title: The Art and Science of Paper
intro: Notes and observations from Toshali’s Frugal Science Lab Notebook.
paragraphs: Being the foodie that I am, the highlight of the lecture was definitely pasta. I will definitely try and experiment with pasta and paper!
It was interesting to learn that we still don’t have mathematical equations to define the tensile strength of paper. I also tried tearing up a lot of pages: wet paper makes less noise than dry paper.
Thin paper curls up more than wider paper strips. When we tear paper faster, it makes more sound. I could see more pronounced fibres on wet paper than on dry paper.
Paper is a world of random network fibres! It assumes a helix kind of structure after drying and being hung. Reminds me of the classical DNA structure that we all have studied about!

Could something be done to wet paper to turn it into the original paper? What if I used tea, coffee, or another solvent to wet the paper and then dried it? How can we get the original properties of paper then?

title: Compliant Design / Flexures
intro: Notes and observations from Toshali’s Frugal Science Lab Notebook.
paragraphs: The most intriguing aspect about the lecture this week was making objects that are in the nanometer range!

Using a glue gun, we can make a thin polymer wire that becomes invisible after a certain interval of time as we keep pulling it. The faster we pull, the more it stretches when it is hot. The ends still remain visible; however, in a particular zone it seems to disappear.
Compliant designs can be thought of as monolithic structures that transform inputs to desired outputs through the structure itself.

Blade flexures can move around and bend like torsion too. As the thickness of the blade increases, it becomes difficult to twist it. A notch flexure has a dent between the ends that changes these constraints.
Could logic gates be built using compliant design mechanisms? Papers online suggest that mechanical structures have implemented NOT, AND, and OR gates.
